label: Lines under load: straps, winch cable, bent trees
summary: A stretched recovery strap or a sapling bent under a fallen tree stores energy, and a winch cable under load can snap with enough force to kill. When a line, hook, shackle or anchor gives way, or a spring pole is cut, it recoils with any metal fittings on it, and people have died, in one case when a tow hook came straight through a windscreen. For coil and torsion springs, see Spring under tension.
signs: Any strap, rope, cable or chain pulled tight between a vehicle and a stuck vehicle, tree or anchor
Recovery (snatch) straps: built to stretch, so they store energy. Plain tow straps aren't meant to stretch
Pull points not made for recovery: tow balls, tie-down loops, bumpers, brush guards and hooks of unknown rating
Winch cable that is kinked (even if straightened), frayed, glazed or melted, or with fewer than 5 turns of steel (10 of synthetic) left on the drum
Saplings and limbs pinned or bent under a fallen tree, or under a log you're about to cut
A load heavier than the hook, strap or anchor was rated for, such as a truck still coupled to loaded trailers
do: Get passengers out of both vehicles. Keep everyone out of line with the pull and back at least 1.5 times the strap's unstretched length; keep people clear of a winch cable in use
Lay a damper over the middle of the line: a heavy jacket, tarp, blanket or bag. Slack the line off before you move it
Pull only from rated recovery points or the frame, with rated shackles. A strap's breaking strength should be 2 to 3 times the gross vehicle mass (GVM) of the lighter vehicle
Lighten the load first: uncouple any trailers before pulling
Winch slowly from a stationary vehicle, with a tree-trunk protector or strap round any anchor tree
Handle winch rope in heavy leather gloves and use the hook strap, so your fingers stay out of the hook

Spring poles: cut only if you must. Stand well back and make 4–6 shallow cuts about 12 mm (½ in) apart on the inside of the bend, stopping each cut the moment the wood moves. Make the release cut from the top, about 12 mm (½ in) past the last cut, clear of the piece that will spring
Check a recovery strap for damage before every pull. A wet strap is weaker and stretches less than a dry one
dont: Don't hook a strap to a tow ball or tie-down point: they aren't strong enough and can easily break off and cause injury or death
Don't use a recovery strap or bungee cord with a winch, and don't drive the winching vehicle to jerk or take up slack in the cable
Don't touch, push, pull or straddle a loaded winch cable, or let it run through your hands, even in gloves
Don't hook winch cable back onto itself, or replace winch rope with hardware-store rope: it stretches and stores energy
Don't use damaged or worn straps, chains, hooks or other rigging
Don't stand in the path of a spring pole as you release it
ppe: Heavy leather gloves and eye protection for rigging and handling cable
Against recoil, what protects you is distance, staying out of line with the pull, and a damper over the line
firstAid: Control heavy bleeding with firm direct pressure. If that fails on an arm or leg, put a tourniquet 5–10 cm (2–4 in) above the wound and at least 2.5 cm (1 in) above any joint, tighten until bleeding stops and note the time
Leave anything stuck in the body in place and pad around it without pressing on it
After a blow to the head, neck or back, keep them still; confusion, drowsiness or vomiting point to a serious head injury

A hard hit to the chest or belly can bleed inside: watch for tender, swollen or hard areas, severe thirst, blood in vomit and signs of shock (cool clammy skin, confusion, fast breathing); let them rest and give nothing by mouth
